title: Seeking refuge first
hook: recitation begins with refuge from Shaytan, then bismillah (16:98)

segments.voice: Yesterday: tilawah, the Qur'an heard before it's read. Your line was hear it first. Did you listen to one surah recited, and what stayed with you, the words or the voice? Day one hundred fifty-eight.

Watch anyone about to recite the Qur'an, a famous reciter in front of thousands or a nine-year-old at an evening class in Ohio. Before the first verse come two short lines, almost always the same two. People say them the way a pilot runs the checklist before takeoff: quietly, every time, no skipping. The first line isn't from the surah at all. It's a request for protection. The second is the bismillah, which you met on day two. Today: why a recitation starts by asking for shelter, and only then says the name.
screen: `TWO LINES BEFORE THE FIRST VERSE.` → `EVERY TIME, NO SKIPPING.` → `SHELTER FIRST.`

segments.voice: The first line is called the ta'awwudh, from a root that means to seek refuge, to run to someone for cover. The usual words are a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim: I seek refuge in Allah from Shaytan, the rejected one. The habit comes from a verse in Surah an-Nahl, which Pickthall translates: And when thou recitest the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from Satan the outcast. Most scholars read it as a strong recommendation before reciting, and the practice is found in every Muslim community. Why ask for protection right before something good? Islamic teaching says the moment you turn toward the good is exactly when distraction arrives. You open the text and suddenly remember an email. You stand to pray and your mind replays an argument. Muslims understand Shaytan as a real being who whispers, and many also see his work in that ordinary pull away from what matters. Either way, the ta'awwudh is a door closing behind you before you sit down. Then comes the bismillah: in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Scholars point to the order. First you let go of what you don't want to bring in. Then you name what you're entering with. Clearing, then naming. The two lines take about five seconds. And the ta'awwudh travels beyond recitation. A hadith in Bukhari tells of two men quarreling near the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, one red in the face with anger. The Prophet said he knew words that would make the anger leave: a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim. So people say it before reciting, and also in the middle of a bad moment, when a thought won't let go.
screen: `TA'AWWUDH — TO RUN FOR COVER.` · `SEEK REFUGE WHEN YOU RECITE (16:98).` · `CLEAR FIRST, THEN NAME.` · `WORDS FOR A HOT MOMENT.` · then, large: `REFUGE, THEN THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can say the two lines quietly: a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim, and then bismillah ir-rahman ir-rahim. If you don't, just follow the shape. Name one thing that's pulling at you right now, and set it down on a long out-breath. Then say nothing more. Don't recite, don't plan. Stay in the quiet that comes after clearing and naming. The bell holds the time.
Ta'awwudh. Seeking refuge in Allah from Shaytan, the line said before reciting, just before the bismillah. Today's word.
Your line: refuge, then the name. Before one thing you start today, a task, a call, a meal, pause and set down one distraction first. Then begin. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Before reciting the Qur'an, Muslims usually say the ta'awwudh (a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim) and then, at the start of a surah, the bismillah; many also say the ta'awwudh when angry or troubled by a bad thought.

original.note: Arabic: seeking refuge, from the root '-w-dh, the same root as a'udhu, "I seek refuge."

trapdoor: what you thought: a warm-up line before the real recitation.
what it means: a request for shelter from Shaytan, clearing the way before the bismillah names what you begin with.
what a scholar hears: 16:98 grounds it; most jurists call it strongly recommended before recitation; the root '-w-dh also opens Surahs 113 and 114: qul a'udhu.
